data.long_meaning: Derived from the Scandinavian 'Steen', meaning stone, Stina is a name of strength and companionship. In Norse mythology, stones were believed to have protective powers. The name Stina carries the meaning “Strength, Companion” and is chosen by families in Christian traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Biblical tradition and is also used in English, Hebrew, Greek. Parents who choose Stina usually hope their child will grow to embody strength, companion and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Stina total 9, giving a life-path number of 9. Number 9 is linked with Mars and with the qualities of compassion, idealism and generosity.

data.cultural_impact: In the Christian tradition, the name Stina can be connected to the figure of St. Martina of Rome. She was a young girl who was flogged and later beheaded for her faith. Her story is one of courage and steadfastness in the face of persecution, embodied by the name Stina's original meaning of strength.
data.spiritual_significance: The name Stina can be seen as a reminder of the strength and courage that comes from our faith. Like St. Martina, we too are called to stand firm in our beliefs and not waver in the face of adversity. The protective and comforting connotations of the name's Scandinavian roots, where stones are believed to have supernatural powers, can also be seen as a reflection of the shielding and nurturing embrace of God.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Stina, derived from the Scandinavian name Stine, may be interpreted as a symbol of steadfastness and endurance in faith. It embodies the spiritual strength and resilience of a Christian, reminding us to remain steadfast in our beliefs and unwavering in our commitment to God.

historical_references.reference: According to legend, Stina was a 13th century Norwegian nun who was known for her kindness and piety. She was said to have hidden a crucifix in her cloak and carried it with her wherever she went to remind herself of her faith.

Another reference to Stina comes from the 16th century Swedish martyr Stina Nyeborg. She was a peasant woman who was accused of being a witch and was publicly tortured and executed for refusing to renounce her faith. Her story became an inspiration for the Protestant reformer Olaus Petri.
